a positive mutation is more likely in patients with a history of seizures beginning before age of 1 year, normal development before the onset of seizures, exacerbation with fever, ataxia, and/or pyramidal signs or myoclonus, and multiple seizure types.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a positive test for SCN1A is a good predictor of Dravet Syndrome, but a negative test is not a good predictor of not having Dravet Syndrome.
the presence of ≥4 International League against Epilepsy criteria should prompt genetic testing.

a mutation of the SCN1A gene should be considered in any child with suspected Dravets syndrome who has a normal development prior to seizure onset, seizures triggered by fever, and/or a combination of ataxia/pyramidal signs/myoclonus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
clinicians should consider testing for SCN1A mutations in all children with Dravet syndrome and should order SCN1A testing in children with atypical Dravet syndrome.
the presence of at least 4 of the 7 criteria is sufficient to order genetic testing for SCN1A in a patient with suspected Dravets Syndrome.
clinicians should consider genetic testing for SCN1A in any child with suspected Dravett Syndrome, regardless of whether they fulfill all the criteria.
